newsitem.title: UK: Study explains how bacteria survive airless depths.
newsitem.headline: Study explains how bacteria survive airless depths.

text.p: Marine scientists said on Wednesday they may have explained how bacteria can survive, and even thrive, deep in the airless sediments under the sea.
They said burying organic matter -- such as the remains of dead plants or fish -- generated acetate, which the bacteria seemed to like.
John Parkes and colleagues at the University of Bristol in Britain and Norway's University of Bergen did a series of tests to simulate the hot, distant depths under the ocean sediments.
They knew acetate could be a source of carbon -- the basis for all life on Earth -- but analysis of the sediments shows acetate concentrations are low.
The secret could be heat -- and layers of soil do get hotter as they go deeper and nearer the Earth's hot mantle.

"Heating surface coastal marine sediments to simulate increasing temperature during burial produces an increase of over three orders of magnitude in acetate concentrations and increases bacterial activity," they wrote in a report in the science journal Nature.
They also took samples and found more acetate at depths below 150 metres (500 feet), and more bacterial activity there, too.

"Thus, acetate generation from organic matter during burial may explain the presence of a deep bacterial biosphere in marine sediments, and could underpin an even deeper and hotter biosphere than has previously been considered," they concluded.
Scientists have been mystified in recent years by where they can find bacteria. They thrive in hot sulphur springs, deep under the Earth's surface and in the layers of sediment beneath the sea.
Finding such extremophiles, as they are dubbed, raises the possibility that life could exist elsewhere in the universe, where conditions are not so benevolent as the Earth's surface.
